source.title: PRBench: A Standardized Probabilistic Robustness Benchmark
source.authors: Yi Zhang; Zheng Wang; Zhen Chen; Wen-Jie Ruan; Qing Guo; Siddartha Khastgir; C. Maple; Xing-Yu Zhao

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent cutoff, garbling, or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares training methods using empirical train–test generalization errors for probabilistic and adversarial robustness, and gives a stability-based analysis. This is a different target and measure from the listed versions’ natural-label generalization claim.
record.gate_note: Results bear on generalization-error behavior under robustness metrics, but the paper does not test any of V1–V8: its GE is the train–test gap in adversarial or probabilistic robustness, not natural-label test error after fitting arbitrary or natural labels. It reports no random-label memorization experiment, width sweep, image architecture comparison for natural generalization, optimizer or batch-size comparison, dropout study, magnitude-aware sharpness measure, or memorized-example removal experiment.
record.test_reason: The study measures adversarial and probabilistic robustness and their train–test gaps. It does not test any of V1–V8's specific comparisons or interventions. Clean accuracy, algorithmic stability bounds, and objective smoothness alone do not establish any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that adversarial training generally improves both AR and PR, while risk-based training offers higher clean accuracy and lower robustness gaps, and provide a stability-based explanation. They cautiously suggest developing balanced AT-based approaches. Their stronger statements that all RT methods have lower gaps are not universal in their tables; AT-PR is a hybrid with gaps often resembling PGD.
record.recipe_differences: The study benchmarks robustness training methods and measures adversarial/probabilistic train–test gaps; the listed claim versions concern natural-label generalization and other specific interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported PR and robustness-GE results vary with perturbation radius and distribution, dataset, model architecture, training method, attack, and robustness tolerance. The text states RT GE is lower than AT GE across both AR and PR metrics in most comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: Robustness train–test gaps depend on the training objective and evaluation setting. On CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, corruption and CVaR training generally have smaller PR gaps than adversarial methods, with exceptions: at radius 0.08, corruption has a 6.24-point gap versus ALP's 5.93. The broader tables also contain reversals, including several MNIST comparisons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Risk-based training often yields smaller adversarial or probabilistic robustness generalization gaps than adversarial training, with exceptions depending on method, dataset, and perturbation setting.

record.peer_reviewed: Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (accepted by KDD’26; preprint version)
record.problems: The paper presents representative CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 values in the main text and refers to appendix tables and figures for wider coverage. No uncertainty intervals or significance tests are reported for the empirical GE values. The measured gaps concern adversarial/probabilistic robustness, not the natural-label generalization gap in the claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No more than 60 rows retained. Main text tables provide many additional dataset, architecture, method, distribution, and metric results; these are omitted because they remain outside V1–V8 and the retained rows already exemplify the finding for fits_no_version. Appendix Tables 7–11 and Figures 2–5 also contain further robustness metrics and settings.

untested.parts: Coexistence of random-label fitting and natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe; chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test-error changes from widening beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning; optimizer switching and decoupled weight decay.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations that remove their penalty.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, and joint removal of dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight sharpness versus generalization gaps and competing norm or margin measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: Change the reader's tests/T2 classification to discusses/T6. The mismatch concerns the specific comparisons named by V1–V8, not simply whether evaluation uses perturbed inputs. Objective smoothness and input-space decision-boundary analysis do not measure V7's magnitude-aware weight sharpness. Additional robustness results are already declared in rows_left_out and require no missing entries.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label fitting or natural-label held-out accuracy comparison.
No width sweep around interpolation or natural-label test-error measurement.
All models use SGD with momentum; no adaptive optimizer comparison.
No batch-size comparison or fixed-epoch large-batch evaluation.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or norm/margin measure comparison.
